subject: oSCR - Density models with categorical covariates

messages.author: 62f7669158940be6
messages.subject: oSCR - Density models with categorical covariates
parts:
Hello!

I'm trying run the model below:
oSCR.fit(list(D ~ MapBiomas, p0 ~ 1 ,sig ~ 1),sf,ss,encmod="P" ,se=T)

the "MapBiomas" is a categorical co-variate obtained through a raster file of land cover/use, using the extract function. 

So is how my ssDF looks like, each number represents a categorical land cover/use with a total of 6 levels (3,9,12,15,21,33)

             X           Y       Tr MapBiomas   
46  514454 6667840  1    21
47  514704 6667840  1    24
48  514954 6667840  1    21
49  515204 6667840  1    12
50  515454 6667840  1    12
51  515704 6667840  1    21
52  515954 6667840  1    12
[omitted  rows]

When I run the model, everything seems good at first, but soon returns a erro message:

Fitting model: D~MapBiomas, p0~1, sigma~1, asu~1 
Using ll function 'msLL.sex' 
Hold on tight!
2019-06-21 12:36:46
p0.(Intercept) |  sig.(Intercept) |  d0.(Intercept) |  d.beta.MapBiomas9 |  d.beta.MapBiomas12 |  d.beta.MapBiomas15 |  d.beta.MapBiomas21 |  d.beta.MapBiomas33 |  psi.constant |  
 
Error in dm.den[[s]] %*% d.beta : non-conformable arguments

I think that message means a problem with my co-variate, It's possible run a model with a categorical co-variate ?
With others continuous co-variates the models runs.

Thanks in advance!

Paula

messages.author: 527d9b3ec7deff2d
messages.subject: Re: oSCR - Density models with categorical covariates
parts:
Hi Paula,

Could you provide more details on your study?  Even just the results of calling "scrFrame" to the console.

6 coefficients for the density model is probably too many for most analyses, unless you have a huge trapping grid with many captures and large spatial variation in density.

messages.subject: Re: [oscr_package] Re: oSCR - Density models with categorical covariates
parts: Unfortunately that is too sparse of a data set for estimating such density variation.  Session-specific parameters are probably not a good idea either.  But the posterior distributions of density in each year (see predict.oSCR) could be used to generate hypotheses that are further explored.
